topics.title: Types of Clients: Individuals, Businesses, Trusts, Estates and Charities
topics.reading:
Before you can recommend anything, you must know who the client legally is. The exam tests three questions for each type of client: Who is liable for the entity's debts? How is the income taxed? Who has authority to give trading instructions, and what document proves it?

Individuals and joint accounts

An individual account has one owner, who alone can trade (unless a third party receives written trading authorization or a power of attorney). Joint accounts, covered elsewhere, add co-owners. The individual is taxed on all account income on his or her own return.

Business entities

EntityOwner liabilityTaxationTrading authority / document
Sole proprietorshipUnlimited — business and personal assets are onePass-through; business profit reported on owner's Form 1040 (Schedule C) and subject to self-employment taxThe owner
General partnershipUnlimited, joint and several, for all general partnersPass-through; partnership files an information return and issues each partner a Schedule K-1Partnership agreement (and a partnership account agreement) naming who may trade
Limited partnershipAt least one general partner with unlimited liability; limited partners liable only up to their investmentPass-through (K-1)The general partner manages; limited partners are passive and lose limited liability if they take part in management
LLCMembers' liability limited to their investmentPass-through by default (multi-member taxed as a partnership; single-member "disregarded"); may elect to be taxed as a corporationOperating agreement names managing members or managers
C corporationShareholders' liability limited to their investmentTaxed at the entity level (flat 21% federal rate); dividends taxed again to shareholders — double taxationCorporate resolution naming the officers authorized to trade; margin trading requires authorization in the charter/bylaws
S corporationLimitedPass-through; no entity-level federal income tax in generalCorporate resolution

An S corporation must meet strict eligibility rules: no more than 100 shareholders, only one class of stock (differences in voting rights are allowed), and shareholders generally must be individuals who are U.S. citizens or residents (plus certain estates and trusts) — no nonresident aliens, partnerships or corporations. Owners get limited liability and single taxation. An LLC offers the same combination with more flexibility and no shareholder limit.

Exam tip: "Limited liability + pass-through taxation" points to an S corporation or LLC. "Double taxation" points only to the C corporation. "Unlimited liability" points to a sole proprietor or a general partner.

Trusts

A trust is a legal arrangement in which a grantor (settlor) transfers assets to a trustee, who manages them for beneficiaries. The trustee has trading authority, and the adviser should obtain a copy of the trust agreement (or a certification of trust) to confirm the trustee's powers and any investment restrictions. The trustee is a fiduciary.

  • Revocable (living) trust — the grantor can change or cancel it. It is a "grantor trust": income is taxed to the grantor, and assets remain in the grantor's estate for estate tax purposes. Its main benefit is avoiding probate.
  • Irrevocable trust — cannot be changed easily. Assets are generally removed from the grantor's estate. The trust itself is usually a separate taxpayer (Form 1041).
  • A simple trust must distribute all income each year; a complex trust may accumulate income, make principal distributions, or give to charity.

Income a trust distributes is generally taxed to the beneficiaries; income it keeps is taxed to the trust at compressed brackets (see the tax topic).

Estates

When a person dies, an estate comes into existence. The executor (named in the will) or administrator (court-appointed when there is no will) has authority over the account. Before trading, the firm needs a certified copy of the death certificate and court documents such as letters testamentary (executor) or letters of administration. Any open orders in the decedent's account are cancelled at death, and the joint-account and TOD rules decide whether assets even pass through the estate. The estate is a separate taxpayer that files Form 1041 for income earned after death.

Foundations and charities

Qualifying charities and private foundations (IRC Section 501(c)(3)) are generally exempt from income tax on investment income — although unrelated business taxable income (for example, from debt-financed investments) can be taxed, and private foundations pay a small excise tax on net investment income and must distribute roughly 5% of assets each year. Because they are tax-exempt, tax-advantaged products such as municipal bonds are unsuitable for them — they would give up yield for a tax benefit they cannot use. Authority to trade comes from the board, usually through a resolution, and investments must follow the governing documents and investment policy statement. Endowments typically have very long (perpetual) time horizons.

Trap: Recommending municipal bonds (or a tax-deferred annuity) to a charity, pension plan, or IRA is a classic unsuitable-recommendation answer. Tax-exempt investors should hold fully taxable, higher-yielding instruments.
keyPoints: Sole proprietors and general partners have unlimited personal liability; LPs, LLC members and shareholders are limited to their investment.
C corporations are taxed twice (21% flat at the entity, then dividends to shareholders); S corps, LLCs and partnerships pass income through (K-1).
S corp limits: 100 or fewer shareholders, one class of stock, no nonresident alien or corporate shareholders.
Corporate accounts need a corporate resolution; margin requires authorization in the charter/bylaws. Partnerships need a partnership agreement.
The trustee has trading authority in a trust; the executor/administrator in an estate (letters testamentary or of administration).
Revocable trust income is taxed to the grantor and assets stay in the estate; irrevocable trusts are usually separate taxpayers.
Charities, foundations, pension plans and IRAs are tax-exempt, so municipal bonds are unsuitable for them.

topics.title: The Client Profile: Goals, Financial Situation, Risk Tolerance and Time Horizon
topics.reading:
A recommendation is suitable only if it fits the client's profile. NASAA expects advisers to make reasonable inquiry into the client's financial situation, investment objectives, tax status, and other relevant information before recommending anything — and to keep that information current. Advisers owe clients a fiduciary duty, so recommendations must be in the client's best interest based on this profile.

Data gathering: financial and nonfinancial information

Information is gathered through questionnaires, interviews, and document review (tax returns, statements, insurance policies, estate documents). It falls into two groups:

  • Financial (quantitative) — income, expenses, assets, liabilities, tax bracket, existing investments, insurance, employee benefits.
  • Nonfinancial (qualitative) — age, marital status, number and ages of dependents, health, employment stability, investment experience, attitudes and values (for example, ESG preferences), and risk attitudes.

If a client refuses to provide financial information, the adviser can still open the account but may base recommendations only on the information available, and should document the refusal. Updating the profile after life events — marriage, divorce, birth, job change, inheritance, retirement — is part of an ongoing duty.

Financial statements for individuals

Personal balance sheet: Assets − Liabilities = Net worth. It is a snapshot at a point in time. Assets are often grouped as cash and equivalents, invested assets, and use (personal) assets such as a home and cars.

Cash flow statement: Income − Expenses = Discretionary (surplus) cash flow over a period. Positive discretionary income is what funds new investments; negative cash flow means the client should fix spending or debt before investing.

Example: A client has a $450,000 home, a $120,000 brokerage account, $30,000 in savings, a $280,000 mortgage and $15,000 in car loans. Net worth = ($450,000 + $120,000 + $30,000) − ($280,000 + $15,000) = $600,000 − $295,000 = $305,000.

Liquidity is the ability to turn an asset into cash quickly without significant loss of value. Most planners recommend an emergency reserve of about 3–6 months of expenses in cash equivalents (savings, money market funds, T-bills) before money goes into riskier, less liquid assets. Real estate, limited partnerships, hedge funds and annuities with surrender charges are illiquid.

Investment objectives

Typical objectives include preservation of capital (safety), current income, growth (capital appreciation), growth and income, speculation, liquidity, and tax advantage. Specific goals — retirement, college funding, buying a home — each have their own time horizon and dollar target.

Time horizon

The time horizon is how long until the money is needed. Longer horizons allow more volatility because there is time to recover from declines; money needed within a few years belongs in stable, liquid investments. A client may have several horizons at once (a down payment in two years, retirement in 25).

Risk tolerance: ability versus willingness

  • Ability (capacity) to take risk is objective: it depends on time horizon, wealth, income stability, liquidity needs and the size of the portfolio relative to the goal.
  • Willingness to take risk is subjective: the client's psychological comfort with volatility and losses, measured by questionnaires and past behavior.

When they conflict, the adviser generally follows the lower of the two and educates the client. A young, wealthy client who panics at any loss has high ability but low willingness; a retiree with modest savings who wants aggressive stocks has high willingness but low ability.

Exam tip: Questions often ask what the adviser should do first. The answer is almost always to gather information (financial and nonfinancial) and determine objectives and risk tolerance before recommending any product.

Constraints

Common constraints are remembered as liquidity, time horizon, taxes, legal/regulatory, and unique circumstances. Unique circumstances include a concentrated stock position, a religious or ethical restriction on certain industries, or a desire to leave a legacy. Taxes matter: a client in a high bracket may favor municipal bonds or tax-deferred accounts, while a client in a low bracket should not.

Trap: Net worth alone does not measure ability to take risk. A client with a large net worth tied up in a home and a business may have little liquidity and limited capacity to absorb investment losses.
keyPoints: Net worth = assets − liabilities (balance sheet, a point in time); discretionary cash flow = income − expenses (over a period).
Liquidity means converting to cash quickly without significant loss; keep 3–6 months of expenses in reserve.
Ability to take risk is objective (horizon, wealth, income, liquidity); willingness is subjective (attitude). Use the lower when they conflict.
Nonfinancial factors: age, marital status, dependents, health, employment, experience, values and attitudes.
Longer time horizon = greater capacity to hold volatile assets.
Constraints: liquidity, time horizon, taxes, legal/regulatory, unique circumstances.
The first step is always gathering client information; update the profile after life events.

topics.title: Behavioral Finance: Investor Biases
topics.reading:
Traditional finance assumes investors are rational. Behavioral finance studies how real people systematically deviate from rational decisions. The Series 65 tests whether you can match a short scenario to the correct bias — and recognize how an adviser can counter it.

Prospect theory and loss aversion

Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory shows that people judge outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, not by total wealth, and that losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains feel good. This is loss aversion. It leads to the disposition effect: investors sell winners too early to "lock in" a gain and hold losers too long, hoping to "get back to even."

The biases you must know

BiasWhat it looks like
AnchoringFixating on an initial number — often the purchase price or a past high. "I'll sell when it gets back to $50, what I paid."
Loss aversionFeeling losses more intensely than gains; refusing to realize a loss even when the investment no longer fits.
OverconfidenceOverestimating one's skill or information; trading too often, concentrating in a few stocks, underestimating risk.
HerdingFollowing the crowd — buying what everyone is buying (bubbles) and selling in a panic when others do.
Mental accountingTreating money differently depending on its source or "bucket" — spending a tax refund or inheritance recklessly while carefully guarding salary savings, or keeping low-yield savings while carrying high-interest credit card debt.
RecencyOverweighting recent events and extrapolating them — expecting last year's hot sector to keep winning, or avoiding stocks right after a crash.
ConfirmationSeeking out information that supports an existing belief and dismissing evidence that contradicts it.
FramingMaking different choices depending on how identical information is presented — "90% chance of success" versus "10% chance of failure."

Related concepts

  • Regret aversion — avoiding decisions for fear they will turn out badly; often leads to inaction or following the crowd.
  • Familiarity / home bias — overweighting employer stock or domestic stocks because they feel familiar.
  • Status quo bias — sticking with default choices, such as never changing a 401(k) allocation.
  • Hindsight bias — believing past events were predictable ("I knew the market would crash"), which feeds overconfidence.

How advisers counter biases

  • A written investment policy statement and a systematic rebalancing rule remove emotion from buy/sell decisions and counter herding and recency.
  • Dollar-cost averaging reduces regret about timing a lump-sum purchase.
  • Presenting information in more than one frame (both probability of success and of failure) counters framing.
  • Evaluating each holding on its future prospects, not its purchase price, counters anchoring and loss aversion. A useful question: "Would you buy this today at this price?"
  • Viewing the portfolio as a whole, rather than as separate "buckets," counters mental accounting.
Exam tip: The keyword in the stem usually gives it away — "purchase price" or "a specific number" suggests anchoring; "everyone is buying" suggests herding; "the last few months" suggests recency; "only reads articles that agree" suggests confirmation; "won't sell at a loss" suggests loss aversion.
Trap: Anchoring and loss aversion often appear together. If the stem emphasizes a reference number the investor fixates on, choose anchoring; if it emphasizes the pain of realizing a loss, choose loss aversion.
keyPoints: Prospect theory: losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains please — loss aversion.
Disposition effect: selling winners too early, holding losers too long.
Anchoring = fixating on a reference number such as purchase price.
Overconfidence = excessive trading and concentration; herding = following the crowd.
Mental accounting = treating money differently by source or bucket.
Recency = extrapolating recent events; confirmation = seeking agreeing information; framing = presentation changes the decision.
Counter biases with an IPS, rule-based rebalancing, and evaluating holdings on future prospects.

topics.title: Capital Market Theory: MPT, CAPM and the Efficient Market Hypothesis
topics.reading:
Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT)

Harry Markowitz's Modern Portfolio Theory holds that investors should evaluate each security by how it affects the whole portfolio's risk and return, not in isolation. Its core assumptions: investors are risk-averse (they demand more expected return for more risk) and risk is measured by standard deviation (volatility). Because securities are not perfectly correlated, combining them reduces portfolio risk without necessarily reducing expected return. The lower the correlation between assets, the greater the diversification benefit; a correlation of −1 gives the maximum benefit, +1 gives none.

The efficient frontier is the curve of portfolios offering the highest expected return for each level of risk (or the lowest risk for each level of return). Portfolios below the frontier are inefficient; portfolios above it are unattainable. Each investor's optimal portfolio is the point on the frontier that matches his or her risk tolerance.

Systematic versus unsystematic risk

  • Unsystematic (diversifiable, specific) risk belongs to one company or industry — a lawsuit, a failed product, a strike. Diversification can nearly eliminate it.
  • Systematic (market, nondiversifiable) risk affects all securities — recessions, interest rate changes, inflation, war. It cannot be diversified away and is measured by beta.

Since unsystematic risk can be removed for free through diversification, the market rewards investors only for bearing systematic risk.

Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)

Expected (required) return = Risk-free rate + Beta × (Market return − Risk-free rate)

The term (Rm − rf) is the market risk premium. Beta measures a security's sensitivity to market movements: beta 1.0 moves with the market, above 1.0 is more volatile (aggressive), below 1.0 less volatile (defensive). The risk-free rate is usually the yield on Treasury bills.

Worked example: T-bills yield 3%, the market is expected to return 10%, and a stock's beta is 1.4. Required return = 3% + 1.4 × (10% − 3%) = 3% + 9.8% = 12.8%. If analysts expect the stock to return 15%, it offers 2.2% more than CAPM requires — a positive alpha, suggesting the stock is undervalued.

Second example: Risk-free 4%, market 9%, beta 0.8. Required return = 4% + 0.8 × 5% = 8%.

Security Market Line (SML) and Capital Market Line (CML)

The SML is CAPM drawn as a graph: expected return on the vertical axis, beta on the horizontal axis. It crosses the vertical axis at the risk-free rate (beta 0) and passes through the market return at beta 1.0. A security plotting above the SML offers more return than its risk requires (undervalued, positive alpha); one plotting below is overvalued (negative alpha). The CML, by contrast, plots efficient portfolios against standard deviation (total risk), combining the risk-free asset with the market portfolio.

Exam tip: SML → beta (systematic risk), individual securities. CML → standard deviation (total risk), efficient portfolios.

Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH)

The EMH says prices quickly reflect available information, so consistently earning above-market, risk-adjusted returns is not possible. Related is the random walk theory: price changes are unpredictable.

FormPrices reflectWhat is useless
WeakAll past market data (prices and volume)Technical analysis
Semi-strongAll public information (past prices plus financial statements, news)Technical and fundamental analysis; only inside information could help
StrongAll information, public and private (inside)Everything, even inside information

Each stronger form includes the weaker forms. The practical implication of believing in efficient markets is passive investing: low-cost index funds and buy-and-hold rather than stock picking and market timing.

Trap: Under the semi-strong form, fundamental analysis cannot beat the market, but trading on material nonpublic information could (though it is illegal). Only the strong form says even insiders cannot profit.
keyPoints: MPT: evaluate securities by their effect on the whole portfolio; risk = standard deviation; lower correlation = more diversification benefit.
Efficient frontier = highest expected return for each level of risk; portfolios below it are inefficient.
Diversification removes unsystematic risk only; systematic (market) risk is measured by beta.
CAPM: expected return = rf + β(Rm − rf); (Rm − rf) is the market risk premium.
SML plots return vs beta; above the SML = undervalued (positive alpha). CML plots return vs standard deviation.
EMH: weak defeats technical analysis; semi-strong defeats technical and fundamental; strong defeats even inside information.
Believers in efficient markets favor passive indexing.

topics.title: Portfolio Management Styles: Asset Allocation, Active vs Passive, Growth vs Value
topics.reading:
Asset allocation

Asset allocation — how a portfolio is divided among stocks, bonds, cash and alternatives — is the single most important driver of the variability of portfolio returns, more than security selection or market timing.

  • Strategic asset allocation sets long-term target percentages based on the client's objectives, risk tolerance and time horizon (for example, 60% stocks / 35% bonds / 5% cash). The portfolio is periodically rebalanced back to the targets. It is a long-term, passive-leaning discipline.
  • Tactical asset allocation makes short-term deviations from the strategic targets to exploit perceived opportunities (for example, moving to 70% stocks because the manager expects a rally). It is an active strategy and a form of market timing.

Rebalancing restores target weights. If stocks rise from 60% to 70% of a portfolio, rebalancing sells stocks and buys bonds — effectively "selling high and buying low." Rebalancing can be calendar-based (quarterly, annually) or threshold-based (when a class drifts more than, say, 5 percentage points). In taxable accounts it may generate capital gains.

A common rule of thumb for stock allocation is "100 minus age" (a 40-year-old would hold about 60% stocks), though modern variations use 110 or 120 because people live longer. Target-date (lifecycle) funds automatically shift from stocks to bonds as the target date approaches — the "glide path."

Active versus passive management

ActivePassive
BeliefMarkets are not fully efficient; skill can add valueMarkets are efficient; hard to beat after costs
MethodsSecurity selection, market timing, sector rotation, tactical allocationIndexing, buy-and-hold
Costs and turnoverHigher expenses, higher turnover, less tax-efficientLow expenses, low turnover, tax-efficient
GoalBeat a benchmark (positive alpha)Match a benchmark

Buy-and-hold purchases securities and holds them through market cycles, minimizing transaction costs and deferring capital gains taxes. Indexing replicates a benchmark such as the S&P 500 through index mutual funds or ETFs. A core-satellite approach blends the two: a passive index core with actively managed satellite positions.

Growth versus value

  • Growth investors buy companies whose earnings are expected to grow faster than average. These stocks typically have high P/E and price-to-book ratios, low or no dividends, and higher volatility. They are often in technology or emerging industries.
  • Value investors buy stocks that appear underpriced relative to fundamentals — low P/E and price-to-book ratios, often higher dividend yields, and frequently out of favor. Value investing is often contrarian.

Income versus capital appreciation

An income strategy emphasizes current cash flow: bonds, preferred stock, utilities, REITs, dividend-paying common stock. A capital appreciation (growth) strategy emphasizes increase in principal and suits long time horizons. Growth and income blends the two, and preservation of capital emphasizes safety through Treasuries, CDs and money market funds.

Diversification and sector rotation

Diversification spreads investments across and within asset classes, industries, geographic regions, and issuers to reduce unsystematic risk. Sector rotation is an active strategy that shifts money among industries based on the stage of the business cycle — for example, into cyclical sectors (consumer discretionary, industrials, technology) in early expansion, and into defensive sectors (utilities, consumer staples, health care) as a contraction approaches.

Exam tip: Tactical allocation, sector rotation and market timing are all active. Strategic allocation with periodic rebalancing, buy-and-hold, and indexing are the passive side.
Trap: Rebalancing a strategic portfolio is not tactical allocation. Returning to the same long-term target is strategic; deliberately moving away from the target to exploit a forecast is tactical.
keyPoints: Asset allocation is the main driver of portfolio return variability.
Strategic allocation = long-term targets with periodic rebalancing; tactical = short-term deviations to exploit forecasts (active).
Rebalancing sells what has risen and buys what has fallen to restore target weights.
Passive (indexing, buy-and-hold) = low cost, low turnover, tax-efficient; active tries to beat the benchmark.
Growth stocks: high P/E and P/B, low dividends; value stocks: low P/E and P/B, higher dividends, often contrarian.
Sector rotation shifts among industries by business cycle stage — defensive sectors: utilities, staples, health care.
Diversification reduces unsystematic risk, not market risk.

topics.title: Portfolio Techniques: Dollar-Cost Averaging, Formula Plans, Leverage and Bond Ladders
topics.reading:
Dollar-cost averaging (DCA)

With dollar-cost averaging, the investor invests a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals regardless of price. The fixed dollars buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when prices are high. As long as prices fluctuate, the average cost per share will be lower than the average price per share.

Worked example: An investor puts $600 into a fund each month for three months.

MonthInvestmentPriceShares bought
1$600$2030
2$600$1540
3$600$3020
Total$1,80090

Average cost per share = total dollars ÷ total shares = $1,800 ÷ 90 = $20.00.
Average price per share = sum of prices ÷ number of purchases = ($20 + $15 + $30) ÷ 3 = $21.67.

DCA does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss in a declining market. It works best for investors with a long horizon who can keep investing through downturns, and it reduces the risk of investing a lump sum at a market peak. Automatic 401(k) payroll contributions are a natural form of DCA.

Trap: Buying a fixed number of shares each period is not dollar-cost averaging — the average cost then equals the average price. DCA requires a fixed dollar amount.

Formula investing: constant ratio and constant dollar

  • Constant ratio plan — maintain a fixed percentage split between stocks and bonds (for example, 50/50). When stocks rise above 50%, sell stocks and buy bonds; when they fall below, do the reverse. It is essentially disciplined rebalancing.
  • Constant dollar plan — keep a fixed dollar amount in stocks (for example, $100,000). Gains above that amount are skimmed off into bonds or cash; shortfalls are made up from the bond/cash side.

Both force the investor to sell high and buy low mechanically, removing emotion.

Leverage

Leverage — investing with borrowed money, usually through a margin account — magnifies both gains and losses. With Regulation T 50% initial margin, a 10% gain in the securities becomes about a 20% gain on the investor's equity (before interest), and a 10% loss becomes about a 20% loss. Interest costs raise the return the investment must earn to break even, and margin calls can force sales at the worst time. Leverage suits only investors with high risk tolerance, and retirement accounts generally cannot use margin. Leveraged and inverse ETFs are designed for short holding periods because of daily reset.

Volatility management

Techniques to control portfolio volatility include diversification across low-correlation assets, holding cash or short-term bonds, rebalancing, buying protective puts or writing covered calls, using stop orders, and choosing low-beta or minimum-volatility funds. Reducing volatility usually reduces expected return as well.

Fixed-income structures: ladder, barbell, bullet

StrategyStructureWhy use it
LadderedEqual amounts maturing at evenly spaced intervals (e.g., every year for 10 years); proceeds are reinvested at the long endReduces interest rate and reinvestment risk, provides regular liquidity, averages yields over time
BarbellConcentrated in short-term and long-term maturities, with little or nothing in the middleLiquidity from the short end plus higher yield from the long end; flexibility if rates change
BulletMaturities concentrated around a single target date, often bought at different timesMatches a known future liability, such as college tuition in a specific year
Exam tip: "Staggered maturities" = ladder. "Short and long, nothing in the middle" = barbell. "All maturing around the same date to meet a specific need" = bullet.

Other techniques

Buy-and-hold and indexing minimize costs and taxes. Hedging with options or short sales limits downside on specific positions. Immunization matches a bond portfolio's duration to the investment horizon so that price risk and reinvestment risk offset.
keyPoints: DCA = fixed dollar amount at regular intervals; average cost per share < average price per share when prices fluctuate.
Average cost = total dollars ÷ total shares; average price = sum of prices ÷ number of purchases.
DCA does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss in a declining market.
Constant ratio = fixed percentage mix (rebalance); constant dollar = fixed dollar amount kept in stocks.
Leverage magnifies gains and losses; unsuitable for low risk tolerance.
Ladder = staggered maturities; barbell = short + long; bullet = maturities concentrated at one target date.
Immunization matches duration to the time horizon.

topics.title: Tax Considerations for Individuals: Capital Gains, Wash Sales and Cost Basis
topics.reading:
Tax rate concepts

  • Marginal tax rate — the rate on the next dollar of income (the client's bracket). Use it to compare taxable and tax-free investments.
  • Effective (average) tax rate — total tax ÷ total income. Always lower than the top marginal rate under a progressive system.
  • Progressive tax — rate rises as income rises (federal income tax, estate and gift tax).
  • Regressive tax — takes a larger percentage of income from lower earners (sales tax, excise taxes, gasoline tax, Social Security payroll tax because of its wage cap).
  • Flat (proportional) tax — the same rate for everyone.

The Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) is a parallel calculation with its own exemption and rates (26% and 28%) that adds back certain preference items; the taxpayer pays the higher of regular tax or AMT. Common AMT triggers on the exam: interest from private activity municipal bonds and the bargain element when incentive stock options are exercised and held.

Capital gains and losses

Gain or loss = sale proceeds − cost basis. Short-term = held one year or less, taxed as ordinary income. Long-term = held more than one year, taxed at preferential rates of 0%, 15% or 20%, plus a 3.8% net investment income tax for high earners.

Netting: net short-term gains against short-term losses and long-term gains against long-term losses, then net the two results against each other. A net capital loss may offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year ($1,500 if married filing separately); any excess carries forward indefinitely, keeping its short- or long-term character.

Example: A client has $4,000 of short-term gains, $2,000 of short-term losses, $3,000 of long-term gains and $12,000 of long-term losses. Net short-term = +$2,000; net long-term = −$9,000; overall = −$7,000. The client deducts $3,000 this year and carries forward $4,000 of long-term loss.

Wash sale rule

A loss is disallowed if the investor buys the same or a substantially identical security (including a call option on it) within 30 days before or after the sale — a 61-day window. The disallowed loss is added to the cost basis of the replacement shares, and the holding period of the old shares carries over, so the loss is deferred, not lost. Buying the security in an IRA within the window also triggers the rule. Buying a different company in the same industry, or a fund tracking a different index, does not. The wash sale rule applies only to losses; selling at a gain and buying back immediately is fine.

Example: Bought 100 shares at $50, sold at $38 on March 10 (a $1,200 loss), bought 100 shares back at $40 on March 25. The loss is disallowed; new basis = $40 + $12 = $52 per share ($5,200).

Cost basis methods

  • FIFO — first in, first out; the IRS default for stocks if no other method is specified. In a rising market it sells the oldest, lowest-cost shares, producing the largest gain.
  • Specific identification — the investor designates which lot to sell (before settlement), allowing high-basis shares to be sold to minimize gains or harvest losses. Gives the most control.
  • Average cost — total cost ÷ total shares; permitted for mutual fund shares (and dividend reinvestment plan shares) and commonly used by fund companies.

Reinvested dividends and capital gains distributions are taxed when paid and add to cost basis. Forgetting them causes double taxation.

Inherited and gifted property

Inherited: basis steps up (or down) to fair market value on the date of death (or the alternate valuation date six months later, if the executor elects it). The holding period is automatically long-term, regardless of how long the heir holds it.

Gifted: the recipient generally takes the donor's basis — carryover basis — and the donor's holding period. But if the FMV on the gift date is below the donor's basis, the double-basis rule applies: use the donor's basis to measure a gain, the (lower) FMV at the gift date to measure a loss, and if the sale price falls between the two, there is no gain and no loss.

Example: Donor's basis $30,000; FMV at gift $22,000. Recipient sells for $35,000 → $5,000 gain. Sells for $18,000 → $4,000 loss. Sells for $26,000 → no gain or loss.

Dividends and interest

Qualified dividends (from U.S. and qualifying foreign corporations, stock held more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date) are taxed at long-term capital gains rates. Nonqualified dividends — including most REIT dividends and money market fund distributions — and interest are taxed as ordinary income. Municipal bond interest is generally exempt from federal tax; Treasury interest is exempt from state and local tax.

Trap: Inherited property is always long-term, even if sold the next day. Gifted property takes the donor's holding period (when carryover basis is used), so it may be short-term.
keyPoints: Long-term = held more than one year (0/15/20% rates); short-term = one year or less (ordinary rates).
Net ST with ST and LT with LT, then combine; net loss offsets up to $3,000 of ordinary income, excess carries forward indefinitely.
Wash sale: repurchase within 30 days before or after a loss sale disallows the loss; it is added to the new shares' basis.
FIFO is the default; specific ID gives the most control; average cost is allowed for mutual fund shares.
Inherited basis = FMV at death (step-up), always long-term. Gifted basis = donor's basis (carryover).
Double-basis rule: if FMV at gift < donor's basis, use donor basis for gains, FMV for losses, no gain/loss in between.
Qualified dividends get LTCG rates; progressive taxes rise with income, regressive taxes (sales, excise, payroll) hit low earners harder.

topics.title: Taxation of Corporations, Trusts and Estates; Gift, Estate and Generation-Skipping Taxes
topics.reading:
C corporation taxation

C corporations pay a flat 21% federal income tax on taxable income. When they distribute after-tax earnings as dividends, shareholders pay tax again — double taxation. To reduce triple taxation when one corporation owns stock in another, a corporation may take a dividends-received deduction (DRD) on dividends from domestic corporations:

Ownership of the paying corporationDRD
Less than 20%50%
20% to less than 80%65%
80% or more (affiliated group)100%

Example: A corporation holding a small stake in another company receives $100,000 of dividends. It excludes 50% ($50,000); the remaining $50,000 is taxed at 21% = $10,500, an effective rate of 10.5%. This is why corporations favor common and preferred stock of other domestic corporations for their cash. Interest income, by contrast, gets no such deduction, and corporations generally find municipal bonds less attractive than individuals in high brackets do.

Corporate capital gains are taxed at the same 21% rate (no preferential long-term rate), and corporate capital losses can offset only capital gains — no $3,000 ordinary-income offset.

Trust and estate income taxation

Nongrantor trusts and estates file Form 1041. Income they distribute generally passes to beneficiaries, who pay the tax; income they retain is taxed to the trust or estate at compressed brackets. The top 37% bracket applies at roughly $16,000 of retained taxable income, compared with more than $600,000 for a single individual (2026 figures; exam items may use slightly older numbers). Because of compressed brackets, trustees often favor distributing income or holding tax-efficient investments such as municipal bonds and low-turnover growth stocks. A revocable (grantor) trust is ignored for income tax purposes; the grantor reports the income.

Gift tax

The donor is responsible for gift tax, not the recipient. Key rules (2026 figures):

  • Annual exclusion: $19,000 per recipient per year. A married couple can gift-split to give $38,000 per recipient. Gifts at or under the exclusion require no gift tax return; gifts above it (or split gifts) require filing Form 709, but tax is owed only after the lifetime exemption is used up.
  • Unlimited exclusions: gifts to a U.S. citizen spouse (unlimited marital deduction), gifts to qualified charities, and tuition or medical expenses paid directly to the school or provider.
  • The recipient takes the donor's carryover basis.

Estate tax and the unified credit

The gift and estate taxes are unified: a single lifetime exemption covers taxable gifts made during life and the estate at death. For 2026 the lifetime exemption is $15 million per person ($30 million per couple), indexed for inflation. The unified credit is the tax credit that shelters this amount. Amounts above the exemption are taxed at rates up to 40%.

The gross estate includes everything the decedent owned or controlled at death: securities, real estate, retirement accounts, the decedent's share of jointly held property, life insurance the decedent owned, and assets in a revocable trust. Deductions include debts, funeral and administration expenses, charitable bequests, and the unlimited marital deduction for property passing to a surviving U.S. citizen spouse. Portability lets a surviving spouse use the deceased spouse's unused exemption if elected on a timely estate tax return.

Ways to shrink a taxable estate: annual exclusion gifts, direct tuition/medical payments, charitable gifts, and irrevocable trusts, including an irrevocable life insurance trust (ILIT) that keeps policy proceeds out of the estate.

Generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax

The GST tax applies to transfers to a skip person — someone two or more generations below the donor, such as a grandchild (or an unrelated person more than 37½ years younger). It is imposed in addition to any gift or estate tax, at the top estate tax rate (40%). Each person has a GST exemption equal to the estate tax exemption ($15 million in 2026), and gifts that qualify for the annual exclusion generally are not subject to it. If the grandchild's parent has already died, the grandchild moves up a generation and is not a skip person.

Exam tip: Gift tax is paid by the giver; the annual exclusion is per recipient; there is no limit on the number of recipients. A couple with three children and six grandchildren could give $38,000 to each of the nine — $342,000 — in one year with no taxable gifts.
Trap: The marital deduction removes the tax at the first spouse's death but does not eliminate it — the assets are included in the surviving spouse's estate later. Also, a gift of appreciated stock gives the recipient carryover basis, whereas holding it until death gives heirs a stepped-up basis.
keyPoints: C corporations pay a flat 21% federal rate; dividends are taxed again to shareholders.
Dividends-received deduction: 50% (<20% owned), 65% (20% to <80%), 100% (80%+) — so corporations favor other corporations' preferred and common stock.
Retained trust and estate income is taxed at compressed brackets — the top 37% rate applies at roughly $16,000.
Gift tax is paid by the donor; 2026 annual exclusion $19,000 per recipient ($38,000 with gift splitting).
Unlimited: gifts to a U.S. citizen spouse, charities, and tuition/medical paid directly to the institution.
Unified lifetime gift/estate exemption $15M per person in 2026 ($30M per couple); top rate 40%; portability for spouses.
GST tax applies to transfers to skip persons (e.g., grandchildren) on top of gift/estate tax.

topics.title: IRAs: Traditional vs. Roth, Rollovers and Distributions
topics.reading:
Why IRAs matter on the exam

The Series 65 tests the IRA rules that drive a recommendation: who may contribute, whether the contribution is deductible, how withdrawals are taxed, and how money moves between accounts without triggering tax.

Contributions: earned income is the key

To contribute to any IRA you need earned income (wages, salary, commissions, bonuses, net self-employment income, and alimony under pre-2019 divorce agreements). Interest, dividends, rental income, pensions and Social Security are not earned income. A nonworking spouse may fund a spousal IRA based on the working spouse's earnings if they file jointly. For 2026 the limit is $7,500 per person (the lesser of that amount or earned income), plus a $1,100 catch-up at age 50 or older. Exam items may use slightly older figures; know the concept. The limit is shared across all of a person's traditional and Roth IRAs. Contributions for a year may be made up to the tax-filing deadline (about April 15 of the next year, not including extensions). Excess contributions face a 6% excise tax each year they remain.

FeatureTraditional IRARoth IRA
Age limit on contributingNone (removed by the SECURE Act)None
Income limit to contributeNoneYes: eligibility phases out at higher MAGI
Deductible?Fully deductible unless the taxpayer (or spouse) is an active participant in an employer plan and MAGI is above the phase-outNever deductible (after-tax dollars)
GrowthTax-deferredTax-free if distribution is qualified
WithdrawalsOrdinary income (except any nondeductible basis)Contributions come out first, tax- and penalty-free
RMDs for ownerYes, beginning at 73None during the original owner's life
Trap: Being covered by a 401(k) never prevents a traditional IRA contribution; it only affects whether the contribution is deductible. If neither spouse is covered by a workplace plan, the deduction is allowed at any income level.

Early withdrawals: 59½ and the exceptions

Taxable distributions before age 59½ generally incur a 10% penalty on top of ordinary income tax. Common exceptions include: death, disability, substantially equal periodic payments (Rule 72(t)), unreimbursed medical expenses above 7.5% of AGI, and, for IRAs specifically, up to $10,000 lifetime for a first-time home purchase, qualified higher-education expenses, and health insurance premiums while unemployed. SECURE 2.0 added others (for example, up to $5,000 per child for birth or adoption). An exception removes the penalty, not the income tax.

The Roth five-year rule and ordering

A Roth distribution of earnings is qualified (entirely tax-free) only if (1) at least five tax years have passed since January 1 of the year of the first contribution to any Roth IRA, and (2) the owner is 59½, disabled, deceased, or using up to $10,000 for a first-time home. Because withdrawals come out in the order contributions, then conversions, then earnings, an owner can always take back regular contributions tax- and penalty-free.

Required minimum distributions

Under SECURE 2.0, RMDs from traditional IRAs and employer plans begin at age 73 (rising to 75 for those born in 1960 or later). The first RMD may be delayed until April 1 of the year after turning 73; every later RMD is due by December 31 (so delaying the first means two taxable distributions in one year). A missed RMD triggers a 25% excise tax, reduced to 10% if corrected promptly. Roth IRAs have no RMDs for the original owner, and since 2024 Roth 401(k)s do not either. A worker who is still employed and not a 5% owner can usually delay RMDs from the current employer's plan until retirement; this exception does not apply to IRAs.

Moving money: transfers vs. rollovers

  • Trustee-to-trustee transfer: money goes directly between custodians; the owner never touches it. No withholding, no limit on frequency, not reported as a distribution.
  • Direct rollover from an employer plan to an IRA: also no withholding and no frequency limit.
  • Indirect (60-day) rollover: the owner receives a check and must deposit it in an eligible account within 60 days, or the amount becomes a taxable distribution (plus penalty if under 59½).

Once per 12 months: an individual may make only one IRA-to-IRA indirect rollover in any 12-month period, counting all of their IRAs together. Transfers, direct rollovers, and Roth conversions do not count.

20% withholding: when a qualified plan (such as a 401(k)) pays an eligible rollover distribution to the participant rather than directly to the new custodian, the plan must withhold 20% for federal tax. To roll over the full amount, the participant must make up the withheld 20% from other funds within 60 days; any portion not replaced is taxable.

Worked example: Maria takes a $100,000 check from her 401(k). She receives $80,000. To avoid tax on any of it, she must deposit $100,000 into an IRA within 60 days, adding $20,000 of her own money; the $20,000 withheld is recovered as a credit when she files. If she deposits only the $80,000, the $20,000 difference is a taxable distribution (and penalized if she is under 59½).

Exam tip: "Direct" or "trustee-to-trustee" is the recommended answer for moving retirement money: no withholding, no 60-day risk, no once-a-year limit.

Roth conversions (traditional to Roth) are permitted at any income level; the converted pre-tax amount is taxable in the year of conversion but not penalized. Each conversion has its own five-year clock for the penalty on early withdrawal of converted amounts.
keyPoints: IRA contributions require earned income; 2026 limit $7,500 plus $1,100 catch-up at 50+ (shared across traditional and Roth).
Workplace plan coverage affects only traditional IRA deductibility, never the right to contribute; Roth eligibility has income limits.
10% penalty before 59½ unless an exception applies (death, disability, 72(t), first home $10,000, higher education, large medical expenses, etc.).
Qualified Roth distribution = 5 tax years since first Roth contribution AND 59½, death, disability or first home; contributions always come out first, tax-free.
RMDs begin at 73 (SECURE 2.0); first one by April 1 of the following year; no RMDs from Roth IRAs for the original owner.
Indirect rollovers must be completed in 60 days; only one IRA-to-IRA indirect rollover per 12 months; transfers are unlimited.
Qualified plans withhold 20% on distributions paid to the participant; direct rollovers avoid withholding.

topics.title: Employer Plans: SEP, SIMPLE, Solo 401(k), Qualified and Nonqualified
topics.reading:
Qualified vs. nonqualified

A qualified plan meets IRS and ERISA requirements in exchange for tax benefits: the employer deducts contributions when made, earnings grow tax-deferred, and employees are taxed only when they take distributions. The price of those benefits is regulation: the plan must be in writing, held in trust for the exclusive benefit of participants, must not discriminate in favor of highly compensated employees, must meet minimum participation and vesting standards, and (in the private sector) is covered by ERISA.

A nonqualified plan skips those rules. It may discriminate, so it is used to reward selected executives. It needs no IRS approval, but the employer generally cannot deduct the cost until the employee includes the money in income, and the plan does not get ERISA's funding and trust protection. Examples:

  • Deferred compensation plans: the executive agrees to defer salary or bonus until retirement. The plan is usually an unfunded promise; the deferred amounts remain assets of the employer, so the executive is an unsecured general creditor if the company fails. This makes the employer's financial strength a key risk.
  • Split-dollar life insurance: employer and employee share the premiums, cash value and death benefit of a permanent life policy.

Defined benefit vs. defined contribution

Defined benefit (pension)Defined contribution
What is promisedA specific benefit at retirement, usually from a formula of salary and years of serviceOnly the contribution; the benefit is whatever the account grows to
Investment riskEmployerEmployee
FundingActuary determines required contributions; PBGC insures benefitsIndividual accounts for each participant
FavorsOlder, highly paid employees close to retirement (large contributions allowed)Younger employees with a long time horizon
ExamplesTraditional pension, cash balance plan401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing, money purchase, ESOP

Defined contribution plans

  • 401(k): employees make elective salary deferrals (pre-tax or Roth); the employer may match. 2026 deferral limit $24,500, plus $8,000 catch-up at 50+ ($11,250 for ages 60 to 63). Exam items may use older numbers.
  • 403(b) (tax-sheltered annuity): for employees of public schools and 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organizations; invests in annuities or mutual fund custodial accounts. Same deferral limit as the 401(k).
  • 457(b): for state and local government employees (and some nonprofits). Its deferral limit is separate from the 401(k)/403(b) limit, so a worker with both a 403(b) and a 457(b) can defer the full amount to each. Distributions from a governmental 457(b) after separation from service are not subject to the 10% early-withdrawal penalty.
  • Profit-sharing plan: employer contributions are discretionary; the company can skip years. Good for businesses with uneven cash flow.
  • Money purchase plan: the employer must contribute a fixed percentage of pay every year, profitable or not.

Vesting

An employee's own deferrals are always 100% vested. Employer contributions to a defined contribution plan must vest at least as fast as a 3-year cliff (0% until 3 years of service, then 100%) or a 2-to-6-year graded schedule (20% after year 2, adding 20% a year until 100% after year 6). SEP and SIMPLE contributions vest immediately.

Plans for small businesses and the self-employed

  • SEP-IRA: funded by the employer only; contributions up to 25% of compensation, with a 2026 dollar cap of $72,000. Easy to set up, low administration, and contributions are flexible year to year, but the employer must contribute the same percentage for every eligible employee (generally 21 or older, worked for the employer in 3 of the last 5 years, minimal pay). Contributions are 100% vested immediately.
  • SIMPLE IRA: for employers with 100 or fewer employees and no other plan. Employees defer up to $17,000 (2026) plus a $4,000 catch-up ($5,250 for ages 60 to 63). The employer must either match up to 3% of pay or make a 2% nonelective contribution for all eligible employees. Withdrawals within the first two years of participation carry a 25% penalty instead of 10%.
  • Solo (individual) 401(k): for a business owner with no employees other than a spouse. The owner contributes both as employee (the full elective deferral plus catch-up) and as employer (profit-sharing contribution), which often allows a larger total than a SEP at the same income.
Exam tip: Match the plan to the scenario. Older, highly paid owner wanting the biggest deduction: defined benefit. Uneven profits: profit-sharing or SEP. Tiny firm wanting employee deferrals with little paperwork: SIMPLE. Sole proprietor with no staff wanting to shelter the most at modest income: solo 401(k). Rewarding only key executives: nonqualified deferred compensation.
Trap: Nonqualified does not mean illegal or untaxed. Earnings are still tax-deferred to the employee, but the employer's deduction is delayed and the executive bears the employer's credit risk.
keyPoints: Qualified plans: employer deduction now, tax-deferred growth, nondiscrimination, vesting rules, ERISA protection (private sector).
Nonqualified plans may discriminate, need no IRS approval, are not ERISA-protected; deferred comp leaves the executive as an unsecured creditor.
Defined benefit: employer bears investment risk, actuary sets funding, favors older high earners. Defined contribution: employee bears risk.
Profit-sharing contributions are discretionary; money purchase contributions are a mandatory fixed percentage.
403(b) = public schools and 501(c)(3) nonprofits; 457(b) = state/local government, separate deferral limit, no 10% penalty after separation (governmental).
DC vesting of employer money: 3-year cliff or 2-to-6-year graded; employee deferrals, SEP and SIMPLE are always 100% vested.
SEP: employer-only, same percentage for all eligible employees, 2026 cap $72,000. SIMPLE: 100 or fewer employees, 25% penalty in first 2 years.
Solo 401(k): owner with no employees contributes as both employee and employer.

topics.title: ERISA: Fiduciary Duties, 404(c) and Prohibited Transactions
topics.reading:
What ERISA covers

The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) sets minimum standards for private-sector employee benefit plans: retirement plans such as 401(k)s and pensions, as well as welfare plans. It is enforced by the Department of Labor (with the IRS handling tax qualification). ERISA does not apply to plans maintained by federal, state or local governments (for example, a state's 457(b) or a public school 403(b)) or, generally, to church plans, and it does not govern IRAs that individuals open on their own. Nonqualified executive plans are largely outside its protections.

Who is a fiduciary?

Fiduciary status is based on function, not title. A person is a fiduciary to the extent he or she exercises discretionary authority or control over plan management or plan assets, has discretionary responsibility for plan administration, or renders investment advice for a fee. Trustees, plan committees and investment advisers managing plan money are typical fiduciaries. An adviser who selects the fund menu for a 401(k) is a fiduciary for that decision.

The core fiduciary duties

  1. Exclusive purpose (loyalty): act solely in the interest of participants and beneficiaries, for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits and paying reasonable plan expenses.
  2. Prudence: act with the care, skill, prudence and diligence that a prudent person familiar with such matters would use. Because the standard is measured against someone with expertise, it is called the prudent expert rule, a higher standard than the traditional "prudent man" rule. Prudence is judged by the process followed at the time of the decision, not by hindsight results.
  3. Diversification: diversify plan investments to minimize the risk of large losses unless it is clearly prudent not to.
  4. Follow the plan documents, to the extent they are consistent with ERISA.

A fiduciary who breaches these duties can be personally liable to restore plan losses and disgorge profits. Fiduciaries may delegate (for example, hiring an investment manager), but they remain responsible for prudently selecting and monitoring the delegate.

Section 404(c): participant-directed plans

In a 401(k), participants usually choose their own investments. ERISA Section 404(c) offers a safe harbor: if the plan meets the requirements, plan fiduciaries are not liable for losses that result from a participant's own investment choices. Key requirements:

  • At least three diversified investment alternatives, each with materially different risk and return characteristics, so participants can build a portfolio suited to them.
  • Participants may change investments at least quarterly (more often for more volatile options).
  • Participants receive sufficient information to make informed decisions: descriptions of each option, objectives, risk and return, fees, and notice that the plan intends to comply with 404(c).
  • Participants actually exercise independent control over their accounts.
Trap: 404(c) protects fiduciaries only from the results of the participant's choices. It does not relieve them of the duty to prudently select and monitor the menu of options. Keeping an overpriced or poorly performing fund on the menu is still a fiduciary breach.

For participants who make no choice, fiduciaries get similar relief by investing in a qualified default investment alternative (QDIA) such as a target-date fund, balanced fund or managed account; a money market fund generally does not qualify as a long-term QDIA.

Investment policy statements

An investment policy statement (IPS) is a written document describing the plan's objectives, risk tolerance, time horizon, asset allocation, criteria for selecting investments, benchmarks and procedures for monitoring and replacing managers. ERISA does not strictly require one, but the Department of Labor views an IPS as consistent with and supportive of prudent fiduciary process. Once adopted, fiduciaries are expected to follow it (unless doing so would be imprudent), so an IPS that is ignored can become evidence against the fiduciary. The same concept applies to individual clients: an IPS documents the agreed strategy and gives both parties a yardstick.

Prohibited transactions and parties in interest

ERISA bars certain transactions between a plan and a party in interest, even if the terms are fair. Parties in interest include plan fiduciaries, anyone providing services to the plan, the sponsoring employer, unions whose members are covered, owners of 50% or more of the employer, officers and directors, and relatives (spouse, ancestors, lineal descendants and their spouses) of these persons.

Prohibited transactions include:

  • Sale, exchange or lease of property between the plan and a party in interest.
  • Lending money or extending credit between them.
  • Furnishing goods, services or facilities (other than under an exemption for necessary services at reasonable compensation).
  • Transfer or use of plan assets for the benefit of a party in interest.
  • Fiduciary self-dealing: using plan assets in one's own interest, acting on both sides of a transaction, or receiving kickbacks in connection with plan transactions.

Violations trigger excise taxes and required correction. Example: the owner of the sponsoring company sells a building to the company's pension plan at appraised value. The price is fair, yet the sale is still a prohibited transaction because the owner is a party in interest.

Exam tip: ERISA answers usually hinge on three phrases: "exclusive benefit," "prudent expert," and "at least three options changeable at least quarterly with sufficient information."
keyPoints: ERISA governs private-sector employee benefit plans; not government plans, church plans, or individually opened IRAs.
Fiduciary status is functional: discretionary control over plan assets/administration or investment advice for a fee.
Duties: exclusive benefit, prudent expert standard, diversification, follow plan documents; fiduciaries are personally liable.
404(c) safe harbor: at least 3 diversified options with different risk/return, changes at least quarterly, sufficient information.
404(c) does not relieve fiduciaries of the duty to prudently select and monitor the investment menu.
An IPS is not strictly required but supports prudent process; once adopted it should be followed.
Prohibited transactions: sales, loans, services or asset use between plan and party in interest (fiduciaries, employer, service providers, 50% owners, relatives).

topics.title: Education, Custodial and Health Savings Accounts
topics.reading:
529 plans

Section 529 plans are state-sponsored programs for education funding. There are two kinds:

  • 529 savings plans: the owner invests in portfolios (often age-based) and the value depends on market performance. Money can be used at eligible schools nationwide.
  • Prepaid tuition plans: the owner buys future tuition credits at today's prices, hedging tuition inflation. They typically cover tuition and fees only and often have residency requirements.

Key features of 529 savings plans:

  • Contributions are not federally deductible (many states give a state deduction for their own plan). Earnings grow tax-deferred and are tax-free when used for qualified expenses: college tuition, fees, books, supplies, computers, and room and board for students enrolled at least half-time.
  • K-12 tuition: tax-free withdrawals for elementary and secondary school tuition were long capped at $10,000 per year per beneficiary; 2025 legislation raised the cap to $20,000 beginning in 2026. Exam items may still use $10,000.
  • Nonqualified withdrawals: the earnings portion is taxed as ordinary income plus a 10% penalty (exceptions include the beneficiary's death, disability or receipt of a scholarship).
  • No income limits for contributors; high overall contribution caps set by each state.
  • Owner control: the account owner (usually a parent or grandparent), not the beneficiary, controls the money and may change the beneficiary to another family member without tax consequences. This is a major advantage over custodial accounts.
  • Gift and estate treatment: a contribution is a completed gift to the beneficiary that qualifies for the annual exclusion ($19,000 in 2026). A special five-year election lets a donor contribute up to five years of exclusions at once ($95,000 single or $190,000 for a married couple splitting gifts in 2026) and spread it over five years for gift-tax purposes. The assets are removed from the donor's estate even though the donor keeps control.
  • 529-to-Roth rollover (SECURE 2.0): beginning 2024, unused funds may be rolled into a Roth IRA for the beneficiary, subject to a $35,000 lifetime maximum. The 529 must have been open at least 15 years, contributions made in the last five years (and their earnings) are not eligible, and each year's rollover counts against the beneficiary's annual IRA contribution limit (the beneficiary needs earned income, but Roth income limits do not apply).

Coverdell Education Savings Accounts

  • Maximum $2,000 per year per beneficiary, total from all contributors; contributors are subject to income limits.
  • Contributions are nondeductible and may be made only until the beneficiary turns 18.
  • Funds must be used (or rolled to another family member) by age 30; the age limits do not apply to special-needs beneficiaries.
  • Qualified withdrawals for both K-12 and higher education are tax-free, and the owner may self-direct investments broadly.

UTMA and UGMA custodial accounts

Under the Uniform Gifts (or Transfers) to Minors Acts, an adult gives assets to a minor through a custodial account:

  • One custodian and one minor per account; no joint minors, no joint custodians. The account uses the minor's Social Security number, and the minor is the legal owner.
  • Gifts are irrevocable. The donor cannot take them back, and the money must be used for the minor's benefit.
  • The custodian manages the account prudently: no margin, no uncovered options or other speculative strategies. The custodian may be reimbursed for reasonable expenses but cannot use the assets for personal benefit or to satisfy a parent's own legal obligation to support the child.
  • The assets pass to the child at the age of majority set by state law, and the child then has full control, regardless of the parent's wishes.
  • UGMA generally allows cash and securities; UTMA also allows other property such as real estate and can let the custodianship run to a later age.
  • Kiddie tax: a child's unearned income above a small annual threshold is taxed at the parents' marginal rate (applies to children under 19, or under 24 if full-time students). The rule prevents shifting investment income to a child's lower bracket.

Health Savings Accounts

  • Eligibility requires coverage under a high-deductible health plan (HDHP) and no disqualifying other coverage (such as Medicare).
  • Triple tax advantage: contributions are deductible (or pre-tax through payroll), growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free.
  • 2026 limits: $4,400 self-only, $8,750 family, plus a $1,000 catch-up at age 55 or older.
  • Nonqualified withdrawals before 65: income tax plus a 20% penalty. After 65: income tax only, so the HSA then works like a traditional IRA for nonmedical spending.
  • No "use it or lose it": balances carry over and belong to the employee even after changing jobs (unlike a health flexible spending account).
Exam tip: If a grandparent wants to fund college, keep control, and reduce the taxable estate, the answer is a 529 plan with the five-year election. If the question stresses the child gaining control at majority, it is describing UTMA/UGMA.
Trap: Coverdell's $2,000 is per beneficiary, not per contributor. Two grandparents cannot each put in $2,000 for the same child.
keyPoints: 529 savings plans: nondeductible federally, tax-free growth and qualified withdrawals, owner keeps control and can change beneficiary.
529 five-year election: front-load five years of annual exclusions ($95,000/$190,000 in 2026); assets leave the donor's estate.
529 K-12 tuition: historically $10,000/year (raised to $20,000 from 2026); nonqualified earnings taxed plus 10% penalty.
529-to-Roth: $35,000 lifetime, 15-year-old account, recent 5 years' contributions excluded, within annual IRA limit.
Coverdell: $2,000/year per beneficiary, contributions until 18, use by 30, income limits on contributors.
UTMA/UGMA: one custodian, one minor, irrevocable gift, minor's SSN, no margin, child controls at majority; kiddie tax applies.
HSA: HDHP required, triple tax advantage, 2026 $4,400/$8,750 + $1,000 at 55; 20% penalty on nonqualified use before 65.

topics.reading:
Forms of ownership

How an account is titled determines who controls it during life and where it goes at death.

FormInterestsAt death of an owner
IndividualOne ownerPasses by will (or intestacy) through probate, unless TOD
Joint tenants with right of survivorship (JTWROS)Equal, undivided interestsAutomatically to surviving owner(s); avoids probate
Tenants in common (TIC)May be unequal (e.g., 70/30)Deceased's share goes to his or her estate, through probate
Community propertyProperty acquired during marriage owned 50/50 by spouses (in community property states)Deceased's half passes by will; both halves typically get a step-up in basis

In any joint account, all owners must sign to transfer securities or close the account, although the firm may accept orders from any one owner. Checks are made out to all owners.

Transfer on death and beneficiary designations

A transfer on death (TOD) registration for securities accounts, or payable on death (POD) for bank accounts, names a beneficiary who receives the assets directly at the owner's death, avoiding probate. The owner retains complete control during life and can change the beneficiary at any time; the beneficiary has no rights until death.

Beneficiary designations on IRAs, 401(k)s, annuities and life insurance work the same way and override the will. A common planning error is an outdated beneficiary form, for example, a former spouse still named on a 401(k). Advisers should review designations after life events such as marriage, divorce, birth or death.

Wills and probate

A will directs the distribution of assets that pass through the probate estate and names an executor. Dying without a will (intestate) means state law decides, and the court appoints an administrator. Probate is the court-supervised process of validating the will, paying debts and taxes and distributing assets. Drawbacks: it can be slow, costly, and it is public. Assets that avoid probate: JTWROS property, TOD/POD accounts, assets with beneficiary designations, and assets titled in a trust. When an account owner dies, the firm freezes an individual account until it receives documents such as letters testamentary and a death certificate.

Trusts

A trust involves a grantor (settlor) who transfers assets, a trustee who manages them under a fiduciary duty, and beneficiaries. To open a trust account, the firm needs the trust agreement to confirm the trustee's authority.

  • Revocable (living) trust: the grantor can change or revoke it and often serves as trustee. It avoids probate and provides continuity if the grantor becomes incapacitated, but because the grantor retains control, the assets remain in the grantor's taxable estate and income is taxed to the grantor. It becomes irrevocable at death.
  • Irrevocable trust: generally cannot be changed once created. Assets transferred (and their future growth) are removed from the grantor's estate, may be protected from creditors, and the trust is usually a separate taxpayer. The cost is loss of control. Transfers into it may be taxable gifts.

Gifts, basis and estate taxes

In 2026 a person may give up to $19,000 per recipient per year ($38,000 with gift splitting) without using lifetime exemption; the lifetime estate and gift exemption is $15 million per person. The donor owes any gift tax. Gifted securities keep the donor's cost basis (carryover basis), while inherited securities receive a stepped-up basis to fair market value at death. Unlimited marital deduction: transfers between U.S.-citizen spouses are not taxed.

QDROs

A qualified domestic relations order (QDRO) is a court order, typically in a divorce, that directs a qualified plan to pay part of a participant's benefit to an alternate payee (spouse, former spouse, child or dependent). Distributions to a former spouse under a QDRO are exempt from the 10% early-withdrawal penalty (though taxable unless rolled over), and the former spouse may roll the money into his or her own IRA. IRAs are divided through a transfer incident to divorce rather than a QDRO.

Donor-advised funds

A donor-advised fund (DAF) is an account at a public charity sponsor. The donor makes an irrevocable contribution, receives an immediate income tax deduction in the year of the gift, and later recommends grants to charities over time. The sponsor has legal control; the donor has advisory privileges. Donating appreciated securities held more than one year typically allows a deduction at fair market value while avoiding capital gains tax. DAFs are popular for "bunching" several years of giving into one high-income year.

Powers of attorney

A power of attorney lets an agent act for a principal. A limited power (such as trading authorization) is restricted in scope; a general power is broad. A standard (nondurable) power ends if the principal becomes incapacitated; a durable power of attorney continues in force during incapacity, which is why it is a core estate planning document. Every power of attorney ends at the principal's death. After death, the executor or administrator takes over.

Trap: "Durable" means it survives incapacity, not death. After death, the agent under any power of attorney has no authority.
Exam tip: Avoid probate: JTWROS, TOD, beneficiary designations, living trust. Reduce estate taxes: irrevocable trust, lifetime gifts, 529 contributions, charitable giving. A revocable trust avoids probate but does not reduce estate taxes.
keyPoints: JTWROS: equal interests, survivor takes automatically, avoids probate. TIC: unequal interests allowed, share goes to estate.
Community property: assets acquired during marriage owned 50/50; both halves usually get a stepped-up basis at first death.
TOD/POD and beneficiary designations avoid probate and override the will; owner keeps full control during life.
Probate is public, slow and costly; intestate means state law distributes the estate.
Revocable trust avoids probate but stays in the taxable estate; irrevocable trust removes assets from the estate at the cost of control.
QDRO splits a qualified plan in divorce; distributions to the alternate payee are exempt from the 10% penalty.
Donor-advised fund: immediate deduction, irrevocable gift, grants recommended later.
Durable POA survives incapacity; all powers of attorney end at death.

topics.title: Orders, Short Sales and Margin
topics.reading:
Quotes: bid and ask

A quote has two sides. The bid is the highest price a dealer (or the market) will pay; the ask (offer) is the lowest price at which someone will sell. A customer buys at the ask and sells at the bid. The difference is the spread, a cost of trading that tends to be narrow for heavily traded securities and wide for thinly traded ones.

Order types

  • Market order: execute immediately at the best available price. Guarantees execution (in a normal market) but not price.
  • Limit order: execute only at the limit price or better. A buy limit is placed below the current market; a sell limit above. Guarantees price but not execution.
  • Stop (stop-loss) order: dormant until the market trades at or through the stop price, then it becomes a market order. A sell stop is placed below the market to protect a long position's profit or limit its loss; a buy stop is placed above the market to protect a short position. Once triggered, the execution price may differ from the stop price, especially in a fast market.
  • Stop-limit order: when the stop is triggered it becomes a limit order, controlling price but risking no execution if the market gaps past the limit.
Below marketAbove market
BuyBuy limitBuy stop
SellSell stopSell limit

Orders may be day orders (expire at the close) or good-till-canceled (GTC). Memory aid for the table: "BLiSS" — Buy Limit and Sell Stop go below the market.

Short sales

A short seller borrows shares through the broker-dealer, sells them, and hopes to buy them back later at a lower price to return to the lender. Short sales must be done in a margin account. Characteristics:

  • Bearish strategy; also used to hedge a long position.
  • Maximum gain: the sale proceeds (if the stock goes to zero). Maximum loss: unlimited, because the price can rise indefinitely.
  • The short seller must pay any dividends to the lender and faces the risk of a short squeeze or a recall of borrowed shares.
  • A buy stop above the market limits the loss.

Margin accounts

Buying on margin means borrowing part of the purchase price from the broker-dealer, which holds the securities as collateral. Opening a margin account requires a credit agreement (terms of the loan and interest), a hypothecation agreement (the customer pledges the securities as collateral and permits the firm to re-pledge them) and, optionally, a loan consent agreement allowing the firm to lend the customer's securities to short sellers. The firm must provide a margin risk disclosure document.

  • Regulation T (Federal Reserve): initial requirement of 50% of the purchase (or short sale) value.
  • FINRA minimum equity of $2,000 to open or to buy on margin.
  • Minimum maintenance (FINRA): equity must stay at or above 25% of market value for long positions and 30% for short positions (for most stocks). Firms may impose higher "house" requirements. If equity falls below, the customer receives a maintenance call; if not met, the firm may liquidate positions, even without notice.

Margin math

Long account: Equity = Long market value − Debit balance.

Example: A customer buys $20,000 of stock, depositing the Reg T $10,000. Debit = $10,000; equity = $10,000. If the stock rises to $30,000, equity = $20,000. If it falls, the maintenance call is triggered when market value falls below Debit ÷ 0.75 = $10,000 ÷ 0.75 = $13,333. At that value equity is $3,333, exactly 25%.

Short account: Equity = Credit balance − Short market value. The credit balance is the sale proceeds plus the Reg T deposit.

Example: A customer sells short $10,000 of stock and deposits $5,000. Credit = $15,000. A maintenance call occurs when short market value rises above Credit ÷ 1.30 = $15,000 ÷ 1.30 ≈ $11,538.

Why margin matters for suitability

Margin magnifies both gains and losses: with 50% margin, a 10% price move produces roughly a 20% change in equity, before interest. The investor pays interest on the debit balance, can lose more than the original deposit, and may be forced to sell at the worst time. Margin is inappropriate for conservative investors, and it is not permitted in IRAs or custodial (UTMA/UGMA) accounts, and generally not in other fiduciary accounts unless the governing document specifically authorizes it.

Exam tip: Stop orders become market orders; stop-limit orders become limit orders. Sell stops protect longs; buy stops protect shorts.
Trap: A buy limit at $40 with the stock at $42 is not triggered by a rise; it waits for the price to fall to $40 or lower. Don't confuse it with a buy stop.
keyPoints: Customers buy at the ask and sell at the bid; the spread is a trading cost that widens with lower liquidity.
Market orders guarantee execution, not price; limit orders guarantee price, not execution.
Buy limit and sell stop are placed below market; sell limit and buy stop above.
Stop orders become market orders when triggered; stop-limit orders become limit orders.
Short sales require a margin account; maximum loss is unlimited; a buy stop limits the loss.
Reg T initial margin 50%; FINRA minimum equity $2,000; maintenance 25% long, 30% short.
Long equity = LMV − debit; long maintenance trigger = debit ÷ 0.75. Short equity = credit − SMV; short trigger = credit ÷ 1.30.
