topics.title: Market Participants, Execution Costs and Best Execution
topics.reading:
Who does what

  • Broker-dealer: a firm that buys and sells securities for customers and for its own account. In a given trade it acts either as a broker or as a dealer, never both.
  • Market maker: a dealer that stands ready to buy and sell a particular security for its own account, continuously publishing a firm two-sided quote (bid and ask). It profits from the spread and provides liquidity.
  • Custodian: the institution (typically a bank, trust company or broker-dealer) that holds client securities and cash in safekeeping, settles trades, collects income and sends statements. Many investment advisers do not hold client assets themselves; they direct trades in accounts held at an independent qualified custodian.
  • Investment adviser: gives advice and may have discretion over accounts, but generally executes trades through a broker-dealer.

Acting as agent vs. principal

Agent (broker)Principal (dealer)
RoleArranges the trade between the customer and another partyBuys from or sells to the customer out of its own inventory
CompensationCommissionMarkup (customer buys) or markdown (customer sells)
RiskNo inventory riskTakes inventory (market) risk
ConfirmationCapacity and commission disclosedCapacity disclosed; markup/markdown disclosed on many trades

A markup is measured from the prevailing market price (generally the inside ask for a customer purchase), not from the dealer's cost. Markups must be fair and reasonable given the security, the size of the trade, market conditions and the services provided. A firm may not charge both a commission and a markup on the same trade.

Example: The inside quote is 20.00 bid, 20.25 ask. A dealer sells to a customer at 20.50. The markup is 20.50 − 20.25 = 0.25 per share. If the customer instead sold to the dealer at 19.80, the markdown is 20.00 − 19.80 = 0.20.

Exchanges vs. over-the-counter

  • Exchanges (such as the NYSE and Nasdaq) are organized, regulated marketplaces with listing standards. Orders interact in an auction-style market, supported by designated market makers or competing market makers, with centralized trade reporting.
  • The over-the-counter (OTC) market is a decentralized dealer network in which prices are negotiated between dealers and customers. Most bonds (corporate, municipal, government) and many unlisted stocks trade OTC. OTC securities are often less liquid, with wider spreads and less transparent pricing.

Transaction costs

The total cost of a trade includes explicit costs (commissions, markups, fees) and implicit costs such as the bid-ask spread and market impact (a large order moving the price). A "commission-free" trade is not cost-free: the investor still pays the spread, and the firm may earn payment for order flow. For mutual funds, costs include sales loads and expense ratios; frequent trading increases costs and taxes.

Best execution

Broker-dealers owe customers best execution: using reasonable diligence to obtain the most favorable terms reasonably available. It is not simply the lowest commission. Factors include price (including any price improvement), speed and likelihood of execution, the size and type of the order, the character of the market, and the reliability and service of the executing firm.

Investment advisers that choose broker-dealers for clients owe the same duty as part of their fiduciary obligation. Related points:

  • Soft dollars: an adviser may pay a commission higher than the lowest available in exchange for research that benefits clients, under the Section 28(e) safe harbor, but must disclose the arrangement and ensure the research benefits clients rather than the adviser's overhead.
  • Directed brokerage: when a client requires the use of a particular broker-dealer, the adviser should disclose that the client may not obtain best execution and may pay more.
  • Wrap fee programs bundle advice, execution and custody for a single asset-based fee; they can be expensive for accounts that trade little.
Exam tip: "Agent = commission; principal = markup or markdown." A firm in a single trade cannot be both.
Trap: Best execution does not require using the cheapest broker. Paying more for better price, speed or research that benefits clients can be consistent with best execution.
keyPoints: A broker-dealer acts as agent (commission) or principal (markup/markdown), never both in the same trade.
Market makers publish firm two-sided quotes and profit from the spread.
Custodians hold client assets, settle trades and send statements; advisers often use independent qualified custodians.
Markups are measured from the prevailing market (inside quote), not dealer cost.
Exchanges are centralized auction markets; OTC is a decentralized negotiated dealer market (most bonds trade OTC).
Trading costs include commissions, markups, the bid-ask spread and market impact.
Best execution = most favorable terms reasonably available (price, speed, likelihood), not simply the lowest commission.

topics.title: Measuring Investment Performance
topics.reading:
Holding period and total return

Holding period return (HPR) = (Ending value − Beginning value + Income) ÷ Beginning value. It measures total return over whatever period the investment was held, regardless of length.

Example: Buy a stock at $50, receive $2 in dividends, sell at $56. HPR = (56 − 50 + 2) ÷ 50 = 8 ÷ 50 = 16%. Of that, 4% is income (dividend yield on cost) and 12% is capital appreciation.

Total return includes both income and price change, usually assuming distributions are reinvested. It is the correct way to compare investments with different mixes of income and growth.

Annualized returns

Returns over different lengths of time must be annualized to be compared. Annualized (compound) return = (1 + HPR)^(1/n) − 1, where n is the number of years.

Example: 21% over two years: (1.21)^(1/2) − 1 = 1.10 − 1 = 10% per year, not 10.5%.

The arithmetic average of annual returns overstates actual results when returns vary; the geometric average (compound annual growth rate) reflects what the investor really earned. Example: +50% then −50%: arithmetic average 0%, but $100 becomes $150 then $75, a true loss of 25%.

Time-weighted vs. dollar-weighted returns

When clients add or withdraw money, two measures can give very different answers.

  • Time-weighted return (TWR) divides the period into subperiods at each cash flow, computes the return for each, and links them geometrically: (1 + r1)(1 + r2)... − 1. It eliminates the effect of the size and timing of deposits and withdrawals, which the manager does not control. It is therefore the standard for evaluating a portfolio manager and comparing managers, and it is required under the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS).
  • Dollar-weighted return is the internal rate of return (IRR): the discount rate that makes the present value of all cash flows (contributions, withdrawals and ending value) equal to the initial investment. It reflects the timing and size of the investor's cash flows, so it measures the investor's actual experience, and is appropriate when the investor (or a manager who controls the flows) decides when money comes in and out.

Example: A fund gains 20% in year 1 and loses 10% in year 2. An investor buys one share at $100, then buys a second share at $120 at the end of year 1; both end at $108. TWR = (1.20)(0.90) − 1 = 8% over two years (about 3.9% per year), regardless of the investor's purchases. The investor's dollar-weighted return is lower (slightly negative here), because more money was invested during the losing year. Had the investor added money before a good year instead, the dollar-weighted return would exceed the time-weighted return.

Exam tip: Judge the manager with time-weighted return; judge the investor's own results (including the effect of their timing) with dollar-weighted return (IRR).

After-tax and inflation-adjusted returns

After-tax return = Pre-tax return × (1 − marginal tax rate). A 6% corporate bond for an investor in the 32% bracket yields 6% × 0.68 = 4.08% after tax. Conversely, tax-equivalent yield = Municipal yield ÷ (1 − tax rate): a 3.4% muni equals 3.4 ÷ 0.68 = 5.0% taxable for the same investor.

Real (inflation-adjusted) return ≈ Nominal return − Inflation rate. A 7% return with 3% inflation is about a 4% real return. (The precise figure is (1.07 ÷ 1.03) − 1 ≈ 3.88%.) Real return measures the change in purchasing power; it can be negative even when nominal return is positive.

Yield measures

Current yield = Annual income ÷ Current market price. A bond paying $50 a year priced at $1,000 has a 5% current yield; if the price falls to $800 the current yield rises to 6.25%. For stocks, dividend yield = annual dividends ÷ market price. Yield ignores price change, so it is only part of total return.

Risk-adjusted return

Two managers with the same return are not equally good if one took far more risk.

  • Sharpe ratio = (Portfolio return − Risk-free rate) ÷ Standard deviation. Measures excess return per unit of total risk; higher is better. Best for evaluating an entire, possibly undiversified portfolio.
  • Treynor ratio = (Portfolio return − Risk-free rate) ÷ Beta. Excess return per unit of systematic risk; used for well-diversified portfolios.
  • Alpha = Actual return − Expected return (from CAPM). Positive alpha means the manager added value beyond what the risk taken would predict.

Example: Fund A returned 12% with standard deviation 16%; Fund B returned 10% with standard deviation 10%; the risk-free rate is 2%. Sharpe A = 10 ÷ 16 = 0.625; Sharpe B = 8 ÷ 10 = 0.80. Fund B delivered better risk-adjusted performance despite its lower return.

Benchmarks

A benchmark should match the portfolio's style and asset class, be specified in advance, and be investable. Common benchmarks: S&P 500 (U.S. large-cap stocks), Russell 2000 (U.S. small-cap), Russell 1000 Growth or Value (style), MSCI EAFE (developed international markets outside the U.S. and Canada), MSCI Emerging Markets, and the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index (investment-grade U.S. bonds). The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a price-weighted index of only 30 stocks and is rarely an appropriate portfolio benchmark.

Trap: Comparing a small-cap growth fund to the S&P 500 (or a bond fund to a stock index) is an inappropriate benchmark and can be misleading in performance advertising.

Annualized return = (1 + HPR)^(1/n) − 1; geometric average is the true compound rate, arithmetic average overstates it.
Time-weighted return removes the effect of client cash flows: use it to evaluate managers (GIPS standard).
Dollar-weighted return = IRR; reflects timing and size of cash flows, i.e., the investor's actual experience.
After-tax return = pretax × (1 − tax rate); tax-equivalent yield = muni yield ÷ (1 − tax rate).
Real return ≈ nominal return − inflation; current yield = annual income ÷ market price.
Sharpe = excess return ÷ standard deviation; Treynor = excess return ÷ beta; alpha = actual − expected (CAPM).
Benchmarks must match the portfolio's asset class and style (S&P 500, Russell 2000, EAFE, Bloomberg Aggregate).
